name: Hofburg Innsbruck
kurzbeschreibung: The Kaiserliche Hofburg Innsbruck enchants as a Habsburg residence featuring the magnificent Riesensaal, Empress Sisi apartments, and Rococo splendour.
preis: Kaiserappartements ab 1.1.2026: 10,50 € regulär, 8 € ermäßigt, unter 19 Jahren frei (Innsbruck Card inkludiert); Maximilian1 und Sonderausstellungen haben eigene Preise
beschreibung:
Overview

The Kaiserliche Hofburg Innsbruck on the edge of the historic old town ranks alongside the Vienna Hofburg and Schloss Schönbrunn as one of the three most significant historical cultural monuments of the Republic of Austria. Originally erected in the 15th century as a sovereign residence for the Tyrolean rulers, the monumental palace complex was transformed in the 18th century under Empress Maria Theresia into a masterpiece of Viennese Late Baroque and Rococo. With its sumptuous Imperial Apartments, the world-famous Riesensaal, and the imperial Court Chapel, the Hofburg conveys a vivid impression of Habsburg splendour in the Alpine region.

History & Architecture

The origins of the complex trace back to Archduke Sigmund den Münzreichen, who ordered the construction of medieval castle fortifications starting in 1460. His successor, Emperor Maximilian I., expanded the residence into a fortified four-wing complex complete with a Late Gothic coat-of-arms tower (Dürer famously captured the Hofburg in two renowned watercolours in 1495). However, the residence owes its present appearance to Maria Theresia: between 1754 and 1773, a magnificent Rococo palace emerged according to plans by Johann Martin Gumpp the Younger and Konstantin von Walter. The occasion for this monumental overhaul was the wedding of her son Archduke Leopold to the Spanish Princess Maria Ludovica in August 1765. The celebrations were overshadowed by the sudden death of Maria Theresia's husband, Emperor Franz I. Stephan; the Empress had his death chamber converted into an austere, deeply poignant Neoclassical memorial chapel. The architectural crown jewel is the 31-metre-long and 13-metre-wide Riesensaal: adorned with monumental ceiling frescoes by Franz Anton Maulbertsch and life-sized portraits of the imperial family, it ranks among Central Europe's grandest festival halls. Additional highlights include the private living quarters of Kaiserin Elisabeth (Sisi), the Gothic Cellar, and the late-medieval bower (Kemenate).

Visit & Getting There

The Kaiserliche Hofburg Innsbruck is open year-round daily from 09:00 to 17:00 (last admission at 16:30). Admission prices for the Imperial Apartments (from 1 January 2026): €10.50 regular, €8 reduced, children and youths under 19 enjoy free admission! Maximilian1 and special exhibitions have their own prices. With the all-inclusive Innsbruck Card, entry is likewise free of charge. Multilingual audio guides (DE, EN, IT, FR, etc.) are included in the ticket price. Travel by public transport: from Innsbruck Central Station (Hauptbahnhof) by bus routes R or F, or tram line 1 to the Museumstraße or Congress stop (approx. 5–8 minutes on foot). The Hofburg is located directly at Rennweg 1 adjacent to the Tiroler Landestheater and the Hofgarten. By car: via the A12 motorway, exit Innsbruck Ost or Mitte, with parking available in the neighbouring Citygarage or Congressgarage.

Tips

The exhibition rooms of the Imperial Apartments and the Riesensaal are fully barrier-free and wheelchair-accessible via modern passenger lifts; loaner wheelchairs are available at the ticket desk. Combine your visit with a relaxing stroll through the directly adjacent Hofgarten or tour the opposite Hofkirche with its famous "Schwarze Mander" bronze statues.
